opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a decision I made overnight. During my PhD at MIT, I spent most of my time building Taichi, a programming language for high-performance computer graphics and simulation. At first it was just a research tool, something to make my own work easier. Then people started using it: researchers, students, and eventually engineers in industry. I realized the project had a life beyond my thesis.

So when I graduated, I had a few paths. The obvious one for many PhDs is academia: become a professor, write papers, advise students. I seriously considered it. But I kept asking myself where I could have the most impact. Papers are wonderful, but much of what I cared about was getting these tools into people's hands and making them robust enough for real use. That kind of engineering, documentation, community building, and long-term maintenance is very hard to sustain in an academic lab, where the incentives point toward the next publication.

A company felt like the right vehicle for that. It let me build a team of full-time people who cared about the same vision, which was making it much easier for anyone to create visual content and simulations. You need resources and focus for that, and a startup gives you both.

Part of it was also personal. I like building things end to end, and I wanted to learn what I didn't know: hiring, product, talking to users, fundraising. A PhD teaches you to go very deep on one problem. A startup forces you to go broad very quickly. I thought if I didn't try it while I was young and had the energy, I'd probably regret it.

And to be honest, I underestimated how hard it would be. But that's probably true of most founders. If you knew everything in advance, you might never start.

r001.rationale: The response says Hu considered academia but preferred getting tools into users’ hands and building a company. It does not say he lacked a compelling academic research direction at graduation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a decision I made all at once. During my PhD at MIT, I built Taichi, which started as a research project for writing high-performance graphics and simulation code. The surprising part was that once I open-sourced it, people I had never met started using it for things I'd never imagined, not just physics simulation, but robotics, computational imaging, even scientific computing in domains I knew nothing about. The GitHub issues and the community discussions were coming from everywhere.

That changed how I thought about impact. In academia, you write a paper, maybe a few hundred people read it carefully, and the code often dies after the conference. But with Taichi, I could see real people hitting real problems every day, and I felt responsible for making it better. The question became: how do I keep this alive and growing in a serious way? A research lab is not the right structure for that. You need engineers, you need long-term maintenance, you need to care about documentation and user experience, which are things reviewers don't reward.

I did consider the other paths. Joining a big tech company would have been comfortable, and staying in academia was something I'd prepared for during my whole PhD. But both would have meant Taichi became a side project. Starting a company was the only way to work on it full time with a team, and to turn a research prototype into infrastructure people could rely on.

There was also a timing element. The gap between what hardware could do and what most programmers could easily express was huge, and it was getting bigger with GPUs becoming common. I felt that if we didn't build this now, someone else would, and maybe in a way that was less open. So in 2019 I took the leap, and I'm still learning what it means to run a company versus run a research project. They're very different jobs.

r001.rationale: The response cites Taichi’s growing user community, the need to maintain it full time, and a hardware-programming opportunity. It does not say Hu lacked a compelling academic research direction at graduation.

astra-6.text: For me, it was about taking research and turning it into something people could actually use. During a PhD, you have a lot of freedom to explore ideas, but there’s still a gap between showing that something works and making it useful in practice. I wanted to work on that next part: building a product, listening to users, and improving it based on the problems they actually have. Starting a company felt like a way to keep exploring technical ideas while taking responsibility for making them work in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he wanted to turn research into a usable product, but does not say that he lacked a compelling academic research direction at graduation.

sol-6.1.text: For me, starting a company was a way to take the ideas I’d worked on during my PhD and turn them into something people could actually use. Research gives you an opportunity to explore what’s possible, but there’s still a lot of work between a promising idea and a useful product. I wanted to work on that whole process—understanding what people need, building something for them, and learning from their feedback. A company seemed like the right setting to do that.
